title: Growing rhubarb
subtitle: A permanent crown that crops reliably from April to June for years
excerpt: Rhubarb is planted as a crown and harvested from April to June each year. Established crowns need little attention beyond an annual mulch of compost, and a well-sited plant will produce for 10 or more years. Forcing under a bucket in February gives earlier, sweeter stems.
sourceNotes: RHS rhubarb growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. Mrs Loudon, The Lady's Country Companion (1845), Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: Excluding light from a rhubarb crown in late winter to produce long, pink, tender stems two to four weeks earlier than outdoor growth. A large pot, bucket, or traditional terracotta forcer is placed over the crown in January or February. Remove the forcer once the stems are harvested; the crown needs a full growing season of light to recover before it can be forced again. Do not force the same crown two years in a row.

content.text: Rhubarb is among the lowest-maintenance crops in the kitchen garden. Plant a crown in a rich, well-drained spot, keep it mulched, pick the stems between April and June, and it will produce reliably for a decade or more.
in late winter gives sweeter stems up to a month early.

Full sun to partial shade. Deep, fertile, well-drained soil. Rhubarb crowns are large; allow 1 m between plants. Rhubarb needs a period of cold to break dormancy each winter; it does not grow well in regions with mild winters. Good UK varieties include Timperley Early (best for forcing), Victoria, and Champagne.

Plant bare-root crowns from autumn to March, or pot-grown plants at any time. Dig a generous hole and incorporate plenty of well-rotted manure or compost. Plant so the bud is just at or slightly below the soil surface; burying the bud deeply causes rot. Firm in well. Add a thick mulch of compost around but not over the bud.

In spring, clear away the mulch and apply a fresh layer of well-rotted manure or compost around the crown. Water in dry spells through summer. Remove any flowering stalks immediately as soon as they appear; letting rhubarb flower weakens the crown. Every five to six years, divide crowns by digging up in winter and splitting with a spade, replanting the outer sections.

Do not harvest in the first year after planting; let the plant establish. From year two onwards, pull stems from April to the end of June. Grasp each stem near the base and pull with a slight twist rather than cutting; this leaves the base intact. Take no more than half the stems at any one visit. Stop harvesting by the end of June; leave the remaining stems through summer and autumn to feed the crown for next year.

attrs.heading: Leaves are poisonous
attrs.body: Rhubarb leaves contain high concentrations of oxalic acid and are toxic to people and animals. Never eat or compost rhubarb leaves; bag and bin them.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main rhubarb problems in UK growing.

items.symptom: Thin, pale, weak stems each year
items.cause: Overcrowded crown, depleted soil, or harvesting too heavily.
items.fix: Apply a generous compost mulch each spring. Harvest no more than half the stems. Consider dividing if the crown is more than five years old.

items.cause: Crown rot, usually caused by planting too deep or waterlogged soil.
items.fix: Dig out and dispose of affected material. Improve drainage. Replant with fresh crowns in a better-drained position, raised if necessary.
